docs.title: Hospital Identity & Access Integration Project
docs.text:
Build it. Break it. Troubleshoot it. Understand it.

Welcome to a beginner-friendly, hands-on project where you will build a small simulated hospital IT environment and gradually integrate a new software application into it.

Safe learning environment

This project uses fictional users and simulated infrastructure. No real hospital systems, patient data, or production credentials are used.

docs.title: Your Mission
docs.text:
Imagine you have joined the technical implementation team of a hospital.

The hospital needs an IT environment that can:

  • manage doctors, nurses, pharmacy staff, and IT users
  • authenticate employees
  • control access to resources
  • support new software applications
  • integrate applications with existing identity systems
  • be investigated when something goes wrong

You will build that environment step by step.

docs.title: What You Will Build
docs.text:
Host Computer
(Windows, macOS, or Linux)
        │
        └── Virtualization Platform
                │
                ├── Windows Server 2022 VM
                │      │
                │      ├── Active Directory
                │      ├── DNS
                │      ├── Users & OUs
                │      ├── Security Groups
                │      └── SMB Access Control
                │
                └── Ubuntu Integration VM
                       │
                       ├── Network Testing
                       ├── DNS Queries
                       ├── LDAP
                       └── Software Integration

The exact virtualization software you use may depend on your host operating system.

For example, you might use VMware Fusion on macOS, VMware Workstation on Windows or Linux, or another virtualization platform capable of running the required virtual machines.

The important part of this project is the architecture and concepts, not the brand of hypervisor.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
By working through the project, you will gain hands-on experience with:

  • virtualization and virtual machines
  • Windows Server 2022
  • Active Directory Domain Services
  • DNS and IP networking
  • Identity and Access Management
  • authentication and authorization
  • Organizational Units and Security Groups
  • SMB and NTFS permissions
  • Ubuntu Linux
  • LDAP
  • service accounts
  • PowerShell
  • troubleshooting
  • enterprise software integration

docs.title: Part 1 — Build the Environment
docs.text:
01. Virtualization Setup Create the virtual machines that will form the hospital environment.

02. Windows Server Prepare the Windows Server that will become the Domain Controller.

03. Networking Configure IP addressing, DNS, connectivity, and time synchronization.

docs.title: Part 2 — Identity & Access
docs.text:
04. Active Directory Build the hospital.local domain and create the hospital identity structure.

05. Access Management Create users, Security Groups, and test authorization.

06. SMB & Permissions Protect hospital resources using group-based access control.

docs.title: Part 3 — Integration
docs.text:
07. Ubuntu Integration Machine Introduce a Linux system that will act as an external integration machine.

08. LDAP Integration Allow an external system to query identities from Active Directory.

docs.title: Coming Next
docs.text:
The project will later expand into:

  • application-level integration
  • SQL and database integration
  • PowerShell automation
  • provisioning and deprovisioning
  • LDAPS / TLS
  • client workstations
  • troubleshooting challenges

docs.title: How This Project Teaches
docs.text:
This is not a "copy commands and hope they work" tutorial.

For each stage, we will ask:

  1. What are we building?
  2. Why is it needed?
  3. How do we configure it?
  4. How do we verify it?
  5. What could go wrong?
  6. What did we learn?

Real problems encountered while building the environment are preserved as troubleshooting exercises.

Authentication vs Authorization

We configured an SMB clinical folder for nurses.

Emma was a member of GG-Nurses and could access the resource.

Marie had a valid Active Directory account but was not a member of the required group, so access was denied.

Both users could have valid identities, but only one was authorized to access the resource.

docs.title: Ready?
docs.text:
Start with Virtualization Setup →

Project status: Work in progress

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
In this lesson, you will create the virtual environment that will host our simulated hospital infrastructure.

By the end, you will have two virtual machines:

  • a Windows Server 2022 VM
  • an Ubuntu integration VM

These machines will later communicate with each other as if they were separate computers inside a hospital network.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
You need a computer capable of running virtual machines.

The host computer can run:

  • Windows
  • macOS
  • Linux

You will also need a virtualisation platform.

Examples include:

  • VMware Fusion
  • VMware Workstation
  • VirtualBox
  • Hyper-V
  • another hypervisor capable of running the required guest operating systems

Note

This project was originally built using VMware Fusion, but VMware Fusion is not required.

The screenshots and menus you see may differ depending on your virtualisation software.

What matters is that you understand the architecture and can create virtual machines that communicate with each other.

docs.title: What Is Virtualisation?
docs.text:
Normally, one physical computer runs one operating system.

Virtualisation allows one physical computer to run several independent computers at the same time.

Your physical computer is called the host.

The software that creates and manages virtual machines is called a hypervisor.

The operating systems running inside the virtual machines are called guest operating systems.

Our environment will look like this:

Physical Computer
        │
        └── Hypervisor
                │
                ├── Windows Server 2022 VM
                │
                └── Ubuntu VM

Each virtual machine gets its own:

  • virtual CPU
  • memory
  • disk
  • network adapter
  • operating system

To the operating system inside the VM, these virtual resources behave much like physical hardware.

docs.title: Host
docs.text: The physical computer running the virtualisation software.

docs.title: Hypervisor
docs.text:
Software that creates and manages virtual machines.

Examples include VMware, VirtualBox, and Hyper-V.

docs.title: Virtual Machine
docs.text: A software-defined computer running inside the host computer.

docs.title: Guest Operating System
docs.text:
The operating system installed inside a virtual machine.

In this project our guest operating systems include Windows Server and Ubuntu.

docs.title: ISO Image
docs.text:
An ISO is a file containing installation media for an operating system.

It acts like a virtual installation DVD.

docs.title: Step 1 - Install a Virtualisation Platform
docs.text:
Choose a hypervisor that is compatible with your host operating system.

Install it using the instructions provided by the vendor.

Once installed, confirm that you can create a new virtual machine.

Architecture compatibility

Before downloading operating-system images, check that the guest operating system architecture is compatible with your computer and hypervisor.

For example, x64 and ARM systems may require different installation images or virtualisation support.

docs.title: Step 2 - Obtain the Operating System Images
docs.text: You will need installation media for:

docs.title: Windows Server 2022
docs.text:
Download a Windows Server 2022 installation ISO from an official Microsoft source.

This server will later provide:

  • Active Directory Domain Services
  • DNS
  • identity management
  • authentication
  • access control

docs.title: Ubuntu
docs.text:
Download a supported Ubuntu LTS installation image from the official Ubuntu source.

Ubuntu will later act as our integration machine.

We will use it to test:

  • network connectivity
  • DNS
  • LDAP
  • application integration

docs.title: Step 3 - Create the Windows Server VM
docs.text:
Create a new virtual machine and attach the Windows Server ISO.

A reasonable starting configuration is:

Resource Suggested Configuration CPU 2 virtual processors Memory 4-6 GB RAM Disk 40-60 GB Network NAT or shared virtual network

These values are not strict requirements.

You may adjust them depending on the resources available on your host computer.

Do not allocate all of your physical computer's CPU or memory to the VM.

docs.title: Step 4 - Create the Ubuntu VM
docs.text:
Create a second virtual machine and attach the Ubuntu ISO.

A reasonable starting configuration is:

Resource Suggested Configuration CPU 2 virtual processors Memory 4 GB RAM Disk 25-40 GB Network Same virtual network as Windows Server

The important part is the network configuration.

Both virtual machines must eventually be able to communicate with each other.

docs.title: Why Must They Share a Network?
docs.text:
Later, Ubuntu will send requests to Windows Server.

For example:

Ubuntu
   │
   │ LDAP request
   │ TCP 389
   ▼
Windows Server
Active Directory

If the two VMs cannot reach each other over the network, the application integration will fail.

For now, simply ensure that both VMs use the same virtual networking mode.

We will examine IP addresses, subnets, gateways, DNS, and connectivity in the Networking lesson.

docs.title: Step 5 - Install the Operating Systems
docs.text:
Start both virtual machines and install their operating systems from the ISO images.

At this stage, the objective is simply to reach a working operating system on each VM.

The Windows Server configuration will be covered in the next lesson.

docs.title: Step 6 - Check Your Environment
docs.text:
You should now have something similar to:

Host Computer
        │
        └── Virtualisation Platform
                │
                ├── Windows Server 2022
                │
                └── Ubuntu

Confirm that:

  • both virtual machines start successfully
  • Windows Server reaches its login screen
  • Ubuntu reaches its login screen
  • both VMs have a virtual network adapter
  • neither VM consumes all of the host computer's resources

docs.title: Optional - Create a Snapshot
docs.text:
If your hypervisor supports snapshots, this is a useful time to create one.

A snapshot records the current state of a virtual machine.

If something breaks later, you may be able to return to this clean state instead of reinstalling the operating system.

A useful snapshot name might be:

Clean OS Installation

Snapshots are useful for labs, but they should not be treated as a replacement for proper backups in production environments.

docs.title: What You Should Understand
docs.text:
Before moving on, make sure you can explain the following in your own words:

What is the difference between a host and a guest?

The host is the physical computer. The guest is an operating system running inside a virtual machine.

What does a hypervisor do?

It creates and manages virtual machines and allocates resources such as CPU, memory, disks, and networking.

Why are we using two virtual machines?

Because we want to simulate separate systems communicating across a network, rather than installing everything on one computer.

Why must Windows Server and Ubuntu be able to communicate?

Because Ubuntu will later behave like an external system integrating with services hosted by Windows Server.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
Without looking at the diagram, try to explain this architecture:

Host
  ↓
Hypervisor
  ↓
Windows Server + Ubuntu
  ↓
Network communication
  ↓
Software integration

If you can explain why each layer exists, you understand the foundation of the project.

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text:
The virtual infrastructure is ready.

Next, we will configure the Windows Server that will become the hospital Domain Controller.

Continue to Windows Server →

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
In this lesson, you will install and prepare Windows Server 2022 for the hospital identity environment.

Later, this server will become the Domain Controller responsible for services such as:

  • Active Directory Domain Services
  • DNS
  • user authentication
  • identity management
  • group-based access control

At this stage, we are only preparing the operating system.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
You should already have:

  • a virtualisation platform installed
  • a Windows Server virtual machine
  • a Windows Server 2022 installation ISO attached to the VM
  • sufficient CPU, memory, and disk resources allocated

If you have not created the VM yet, complete the Virtualisation Setup lesson first.

docs.title: Step 1 - Start the Windows Server VM
docs.text:
Start the virtual machine containing the Windows Server ISO.

The VM should boot into the Windows Server installation environment.

Select your:

  • language
  • time and currency format
  • keyboard layout

Then continue to the installation screen.

docs.title: Step 2 - Choose the Windows Server Edition
docs.text:
Depending on the installation media, several editions may appear.

For a beginner-friendly environment, choose a version that includes:

Desktop Experience

For example:

Windows Server 2022 Standard Evaluation
(Desktop Experience)

docs.title: Desktop Experience vs Server Core
docs.text:
Desktop Experience provides the familiar Windows graphical interface.

Server Core provides a minimal installation without the traditional desktop interface and is normally administered primarily through command-line tools and remote management.

For this project, Desktop Experience makes it easier to explore tools such as:

  • Server Manager
  • Active Directory Users and Computers
  • DNS Manager
  • Computer Management

docs.title: Step 3 - Choose the Installation Type
docs.text:
When Windows asks which type of installation you want, choose:

Custom: Install Microsoft Server Operating System only

A custom installation is appropriate because we are creating a new server rather than upgrading an existing Windows installation.

docs.title: Step 4 - Select the Virtual Disk
docs.text:
Windows will display the virtual disk created for the VM.

Select the available unallocated disk space and continue.

For this learning environment, a virtual disk of approximately 40-60 GB is normally sufficient.

Windows will automatically create the partitions required for the operating system.

docs.title: Step 5 - Complete the Installation
docs.text:
Windows Server will copy files and install the operating system.

The virtual machine may restart several times.

After installation, you will be asked to configure the built-in:

Administrator

account.

Create a strong password that you can remember for the lab.

Warning

Do not reuse real passwords from personal, university, or workplace accounts.

This project should use credentials created specifically for the simulated environment.

docs.title: Step 6 - Sign In
docs.text:
After installation is complete, sign in using the Administrator account.

You should reach the Windows Server desktop.

Server Manager will normally open automatically.

Server Manager is one of the main administration tools used to configure Windows Server roles and features.

docs.title: Step 7 - Inspect the Server
docs.text:
Before changing anything, inspect the current system.

Open:

Server Manager → Local Server

Look for information such as:

  • computer name
  • Windows edition
  • network adapter
  • IP address
  • time zone
  • Windows Firewall status
  • remote management status

The objective is to understand the server's current state before configuring it.

docs.title: Step 8 - Check the Computer Name
docs.text:
Every computer on a network needs a hostname.

You can check the current hostname from Command Prompt:

hostname

You can also use PowerShell:

$env:COMPUTERNAME

The default hostname generated by Windows may not be very meaningful.

Later, you may rename the server to something easier to recognise, such as:

DC01

This naming convention can help identify the machine as the first Domain Controller in the environment.

docs.title: Step 9 - Inspect the Network Configuration
docs.text:
Open Command Prompt and run:

ipconfig

Look for:

  • IPv4 Address
  • Subnet Mask
  • Default Gateway
  • DNS Servers

Do not worry if the address was automatically assigned.

In the next lesson, we will examine how IP addressing, DNS, DHCP and virtual networking affect communication between the Windows Server and Ubuntu machines.

docs.title: Step 10 - Check Internet Connectivity
docs.text:
If your virtualisation network provides internet access, test connectivity.

For example:

ping 8.8.8.8

You can also test DNS resolution:

nslookup microsoft.com

These tests answer two different questions.

ping 8.8.8.8 helps test basic IP connectivity.

nslookup microsoft.com helps verify that DNS name resolution is working.

docs.title: Optional - Create a Snapshot
docs.text:
Once Windows Server is installed and working, consider creating a virtual machine snapshot.

A useful snapshot name could be:

Windows Server Clean Install

This gives you a recovery point before making major configuration changes.

docs.title: What You Should Understand
docs.text:
Before continuing, make sure you can explain:

Why are we using Windows Server instead of normal Windows?

Windows Server provides enterprise services such as Active Directory Domain Services, DNS, centralized authentication, and server roles.

What is Server Manager?

Server Manager is an administration interface used to configure and monitor Windows Server.

Why do we inspect the network before configuring Active Directory?

Active Directory depends heavily on reliable networking and DNS.

If network configuration is incorrect, authentication and directory services may fail later.

Why are we not configuring Active Directory yet?

We are separating the project into layers.

First we establish the server.

Then we configure networking.

After networking is understood and verified, we add the identity services.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Before moving on, confirm that:

  • Windows Server boots successfully
  • you can sign in as Administrator
  • Server Manager opens
  • the server has a hostname
  • the server has an IP address
  • you can inspect its network configuration
  • the virtual network adapter is working

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
Using only the tools available inside Windows Server, find:

  1. your hostname
  2. your IPv4 address
  3. your default gateway
  4. your DNS server
  5. your Windows Server edition

Try to explain what each value represents rather than simply copying it.

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text:
The Windows Server operating system is ready.

Next, we will configure the network so that Windows Server and the Ubuntu integration machine can reliably communicate.

Continue to Networking →

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
In this lesson, you will configure and test the network that connects the Windows Server and Ubuntu virtual machines.

By the end of the lesson, you should understand:

  • IP addresses
  • subnet masks
  • default gateways
  • DHCP
  • static IP addresses
  • NAT
  • DNS
  • basic connectivity testing

You will also prepare the Windows Server for its future role as a Domain Controller.

docs.title: Why Networking Matters
docs.text:
Our environment contains separate virtual machines:

Host Computer
        │
        └── Virtual Network
                │
                ├── Windows Server
                │
                └── Ubuntu

Later, Ubuntu will need to communicate with services running on Windows Server.

For example:

Ubuntu
   │
   │ LDAP request
   │ TCP 389
   ▼
Windows Server
Active Directory

If the network is configured incorrectly, the application may appear to have an authentication or LDAP problem when the real issue is simply connectivity.

This is why networking should be verified before application integration begins.

docs.title: IP Address
docs.text:
An IP address identifies a device on a network.

For example:

192.168.100.10

Think of it as the network address of a computer.

docs.title: Subnet Mask
docs.text:
The subnet mask helps determine which devices belong to the same local network.

A common subnet mask is:

255.255.255.0

This is also written as:

/24

For example:

192.168.100.10/24
192.168.100.20/24

normally belong to the same local subnet.

docs.title: Default Gateway
docs.text:
The default gateway is the device that allows traffic to leave the local network.

For example:

192.168.100.1

If a machine needs to communicate with a destination outside its local subnet, it normally sends the traffic to its default gateway.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
DNS stands for Domain Name System.

DNS translates names into IP addresses.

For example:

microsoft.com
        ↓
IP address

In an Active Directory environment, DNS becomes even more important because computers use DNS to locate services such as Domain Controllers.

docs.title: DHCP
docs.text:
DHCP stands for Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol.

A DHCP server can automatically provide a computer with:

  • an IP address
  • subnet mask
  • default gateway
  • DNS configuration

This is convenient for normal client devices.

However, servers often use static addresses because other systems need to know where to find them consistently.

docs.title: Static IP Address
docs.text:
A static IP address does not change automatically.

A Domain Controller should normally have a predictable address.

For example:

Windows Server
192.168.100.10

Other machines can then consistently contact that server.

docs.title: NAT
docs.text:
NAT stands for Network Address Translation.

Many virtualisation platforms use NAT to allow virtual machines to access external networks through the host computer.

A simplified view looks like:

Virtual Machine
      │
      ▼
Virtual NAT Network
      │
      ▼
Host Computer
      │
      ▼
Internet

The virtual machine has its own private IP address, while the hypervisor translates traffic when it leaves the virtual network.

docs.title: Step 1 - Check the Virtual Network
docs.text:
Before configuring IP addresses, verify that both virtual machines use the same virtual networking mode.

Depending on your hypervisor, you may see options such as:

  • NAT
  • Shared Network
  • Bridged
  • Host-only

For this project, the important requirement is:

Windows Server and Ubuntu must be able to communicate with each other.

Note

The exact names of networking modes vary between VMware, VirtualBox, Hyper-V and other hypervisors.

Focus on the network architecture rather than a specific product interface.

docs.title: Step 2 - Inspect Windows Server Networking
docs.text:
Open Command Prompt or PowerShell on Windows Server.

Run:

ipconfig

For more detailed information:

ipconfig /all

Look for:

  • IPv4 Address
  • Subnet Mask
  • Default Gateway
  • DNS Servers
  • DHCP Enabled

Example:

IPv4 Address:      192.168.100.20
Subnet Mask:       255.255.255.0
Default Gateway:   192.168.100.1

Your values will probably be different.

Do not copy example IP addresses directly into your environment.

docs.title: Step 3 - Inspect Ubuntu Networking
docs.text:
On Ubuntu, open Terminal.

Run:

ip addr

This displays the network interfaces and their IP addresses.

You can also check the routing table:

ip route

You may see something similar to:

default via 192.168.100.1

This identifies the default gateway.

To inspect DNS configuration on many modern Ubuntu systems, use:

resolvectl status

docs.title: Step 4 - Compare the Two Machines
docs.text:
Record the important information from both machines.

For example:

Setting Windows Server Ubuntu IPv4 192.168.100.10 192.168.100.20 Subnet /24 /24 Gateway 192.168.100.1 192.168.100.1 Network 192.168.100.0 192.168.100.0

If both machines are on the same subnet, they should normally be able to communicate directly.

docs.title: Step 5 - Test the Default Gateway
docs.text:
From Windows Server:

ping <gateway-ip>

For example:

ping 192.168.100.1

From Ubuntu:

ping -c 4 <gateway-ip>

If the gateway responds, the local network path is working.

Note

A failed ping does not always prove that a device is unreachable.

Firewalls can block ICMP traffic while other services continue to work.

Ping is one diagnostic tool, not a complete connectivity test.

docs.title: Step 6 - Test Internet Connectivity
docs.text:
An important troubleshooting technique is to separate IP connectivity from DNS resolution.

First, test an external IP address.

Windows:

ping 8.8.8.8

Ubuntu:

ping -c 4 8.8.8.8

If this works, external IP connectivity exists.

Now test a hostname.

Windows:

nslookup microsoft.com

Ubuntu:

nslookup microsoft.com

If the IP test works but the hostname lookup fails, the problem is likely related to DNS rather than basic network connectivity.

docs.title: Step 7 - Give the Windows Server a Static IP
docs.text:
A Domain Controller should have a stable network address.

Before changing anything, record the settings received through DHCP:

  • current IP address
  • subnet mask
  • default gateway
  • DNS server

Then select an appropriate unused address inside the same subnet.

For example:

IP address:      192.168.100.10
Subnet mask:     255.255.255.0
Default gateway: 192.168.100.1

Warning

These are example addresses only.

Your virtual network may use a completely different range.

Always inspect your existing network before selecting a static IP address.

On Windows Server, open:

Server Manager → Local Server → Ethernet

Then open the network adapter properties.

Select:

Internet Protocol Version 4 (TCP/IPv4)

and configure the chosen static address.

docs.title: Why Does the Server Need a Static Address?
docs.text:
Imagine Ubuntu is configured to contact:

192.168.100.10

If DHCP later changes the Windows Server address to:

192.168.100.35

Ubuntu may continue trying to contact the old address.

The integration would fail.

A static IP gives important infrastructure a predictable location.

docs.title: Step 8 - Verify the Static Configuration
docs.text:
After changing the address, run:

ipconfig /all

Confirm that:

  • the expected IPv4 address appears
  • the subnet mask is correct
  • the gateway is correct

Then test the gateway again:

ping <gateway-ip>

And test external connectivity:

ping 8.8.8.8

docs.title: Step 9 - Understand DNS in Active Directory
docs.text:
DNS is particularly important in this project.

Normal internet DNS may resolve names such as:

microsoft.com
ubuntu.com
github.com

Active Directory DNS will later also resolve internal names such as:

hospital.local
dc01.hospital.local

After the server becomes a Domain Controller with DNS installed, domain members should use the Active Directory DNS server so they can locate domain services.

A simplified architecture will eventually look like:

Ubuntu / Client
      │
      │ DNS query
      ▼
Windows Server
Active Directory DNS
      │
      ▼
Domain services

We will configure this further during the Active Directory stage.

docs.title: Step 10 - Test Communication Between the VMs
docs.text:
Now test communication between Windows Server and Ubuntu.

First find Ubuntu's address:

ip addr

From Windows Server:

ping <ubuntu-ip>

Then find the Windows Server address:

ipconfig

From Ubuntu:

ping -c 4 <windows-server-ip>

If both machines can reach each other, the basic network path is ready.

docs.title: A Better Troubleshooting Method
docs.text:
When something does not work, avoid testing everything at once.

Work through the network layer by layer.

docs.title: 1. Does the machine have an IP address?
docs.text:
Windows:

ipconfig

Ubuntu:

ip addr

docs.title: 2. Can it reach its gateway?
docs.text:
Machine
   ↓
Gateway

docs.title: 3. Can it reach another IP address?
docs.text:
Windows Server
      ↓
Ubuntu

docs.title: 4. Can it reach the internet by IP?
docs.text: ping 8.8.8.8

docs.title: 5. Can DNS resolve names?
docs.text: nslookup microsoft.com

docs.title: 6. Can the application port be reached?
docs.text:
Later, we may test specific services such as:

LDAP  → TCP 389
LDAPS → TCP 636
SMB   → TCP 445

This layered approach helps identify where the failure occurs.

docs.title: Common Problems
docs.text: Symptom Possible Cause No IP address Network adapter or DHCP problem Cannot reach gateway Virtual network or IP configuration problem Can reach IP but not hostname DNS problem Windows and Ubuntu cannot communicate Different networks, firewall, or addressing issue Server address changes DHCP still being used Internet works but domain services fail Internal DNS configuration may be incorrect Ping fails but application works ICMP may be blocked by a firewall

docs.title: DHCP vs Static IP
docs.text: A useful way to remember the difference:

docs.title: DHCP
docs.text:
Device starts
     ↓
Requests configuration
     ↓
DHCP provides IP settings

Good for:

  • laptops
  • desktops
  • temporary clients
  • general user devices

docs.title: Static IP
docs.text:
Administrator chooses address
          ↓
Address remains predictable

Commonly used for infrastructure such as:

  • servers
  • Domain Controllers
  • DNS servers
  • network appliances

docs.title: What You Should Understand
docs.text:
Before continuing, make sure you can explain:

What does an IP address do?

It identifies a network interface so other systems know where to send traffic.

What does the subnet mask do?

It helps determine which portion of an IP address identifies the network and which portion identifies the host.

What is the default gateway?

It provides a route toward destinations outside the local subnet.

What does DHCP do?

It automatically provides network configuration to clients.

Why do we give the Domain Controller a static IP?

Because other systems need a predictable address for services such as DNS and authentication.

What does DNS do?

It resolves names into IP addresses and, in Active Directory, helps systems locate domain services.

What does NAT do?

It translates network traffic between address spaces, allowing virtual machines on private networks to communicate with external networks through the host or hypervisor.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Before moving on, confirm that:

  • Windows Server has an IP address
  • Ubuntu has an IP address
  • both machines are on compatible virtual networks
  • you know the subnet mask
  • you know the default gateway
  • Windows Server has a stable IP address
  • the machines can test local connectivity
  • DNS resolution can be tested
  • you understand the difference between DHCP and static addressing

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
Without looking back at the definitions, explain what happens when Ubuntu tries to communicate with the Windows Server.

Use these terms:

  • IP address
  • subnet
  • network adapter
  • DNS
  • gateway

Then answer this troubleshooting scenario:

ping 8.8.8.8
SUCCESS

nslookup microsoft.com
FAIL

Which network service would you investigate first?

Answer: DNS.

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text:
The network foundation is ready.

Next, we will turn Windows Server into the identity system for the simulated hospital by installing and configuring Active Directory Domain Services.

Continue to Active Directory →

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
In this lesson, you will turn the Windows Server into a Domain Controller by installing and configuring Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS).

By the end of the lesson, you should understand:

  • what Active Directory is
  • what a domain is
  • what a Domain Controller does
  • what Active Directory Domain Services provides
  • why DNS is critical to Active Directory
  • what a forest is
  • what Organizational Units are
  • how to verify that Active Directory is working

docs.title: Where We Are
docs.text:
So far, the environment contains two virtual machines connected through a virtual network:

Host Computer
        │
        └── Virtual Network
                │
                ├── Windows Server
                │      └── Static IP
                │
                └── Ubuntu

The Windows Server currently behaves like a normal standalone server.

In this lesson, we will add an identity system:

Windows Server
      │
      ├── Active Directory Domain Services
      ├── DNS
      └── Domain Controller

Later, users, applications and other machines will be able to use this server for identity and authentication.

docs.title: What Is Active Directory?
docs.text:
Active Directory is Microsoft's directory technology for centrally managing identities and resources in an enterprise environment.

Instead of managing every user separately on every computer, an organisation can maintain identities centrally.

For example, a hospital may have:

Active Directory
      │
      ├── Doctors
      ├── Nurses
      ├── Pharmacy Staff
      ├── IT Staff
      └── Service Accounts

Applications and computers can then use this directory to determine who a user is and what resources they may access.

docs.title: What Is Active Directory Domain Services?
docs.text:
Active Directory Domain Services, usually shortened to AD DS, is the Windows Server role that provides the directory service.

AD DS stores information about objects such as:

  • users
  • computers
  • groups
  • Organizational Units
  • service accounts
  • policies

It also supports authentication and centralized identity management.

docs.title: Authentication vs Authorization
docs.text: These two concepts are important throughout this project.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Authentication answers:

Who are you?

For example:

Username + Password
        ↓
Active Directory
        ↓
Identity verified

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
Authorization answers:

What are you allowed to access?

For example:

Emma Wilson
     │
     ├── Valid account
     │
     └── Member of Nurses group
              ↓
       Access clinical folder

A user can be successfully authenticated but still not be authorized to access a particular resource.

docs.title: What Is a Domain?
docs.text:
A domain is a logical administrative boundary containing identities and computers managed through Active Directory.

For this simulated environment, we will use:

hospital.local

A user may eventually have an identity such as:

emma@hospital.local

or may sign in using a domain-qualified username such as:

HOSPITAL\emma

Note

hospital.local is used here only as a simple learning-domain example.

Production organisations normally choose domain naming based on their real DNS and identity architecture rather than copying this lab name.

docs.title: What Is a Domain Controller?
docs.text:
A Domain Controller, or DC, is a server running Active Directory Domain Services for a domain.

It helps provide services such as:

  • authentication
  • directory queries
  • identity management
  • security policy
  • group membership information
  • service discovery through DNS

Our architecture will become:

Ubuntu / Client
       │
       │ Authentication or directory request
       ▼
Windows Server
Domain Controller
       │
       └── Active Directory

docs.title: Why Does DNS Matter?
docs.text:
Active Directory depends heavily on DNS.

Clients do not simply need to know an IP address.

They need to discover services such as Domain Controllers.

A client might ask:

Where is the Domain Controller
for hospital.local?
```

DNS helps provide that information.

That is why a system can have working internet access but still fail to join or use an Active Directory domain if its DNS configuration is incorrect.

---

## Before You Start

Before installing Active Directory, confirm that:

- Windows Server starts correctly
- the server has a stable IP address
- the subnet mask is correct
- the default gateway is correct
- basic network connectivity works
- the server time is reasonably accurate

You can inspect networking with:

~~~powershell
ipconfig /all

You can check the hostname with:

hostname

docs.title: Step 1 - Open Server Manager
docs.text:
Sign in to Windows Server using the local Administrator account.

Open:

Server Manager

Then select:

Manage → Add Roles and Features

This wizard allows Windows Server roles to be installed.

docs.title: Step 2 - Choose the Installation Type
docs.text:
Select:

Role-based or feature-based installation

This option is used when adding a server role to the current Windows Server.

Continue to the server selection screen.

docs.title: Step 3 - Select the Server
docs.text:
Select the current Windows Server from the server pool.

Confirm that you are installing the role on the intended machine.

Then continue.

docs.title: Step 4 - Install Active Directory Domain Services
docs.text:
From the list of server roles, select:

Active Directory Domain Services

Windows may ask to install additional management tools required by AD DS.

Accept the required features.

Then continue through the wizard.

At this point, we are installing the software required to provide Active Directory.

We have not created the domain yet.

docs.title: Step 5 - Complete the AD DS Role Installation
docs.text:
Review the selected options and begin the installation.

When the role installation finishes, Server Manager should display a notification indicating that additional configuration is required.

The server now contains the AD DS software, but it is not yet acting as a Domain Controller.

That happens during promotion.

docs.title: What Does “Promote This Server” Mean?
docs.text:
Installing AD DS and creating a Domain Controller are related but different steps.

Install AD DS role
        ↓
Server gains directory-service software
        ↓
Promote server
        ↓
Server becomes Domain Controller

Promotion configures the server to provide Active Directory for a domain.

docs.title: Step 6 - Promote the Server to a Domain Controller
docs.text:
In Server Manager, select the notification flag.

Choose:

Promote this server to a domain controller

The Active Directory Domain Services Configuration Wizard will open.

docs.title: Step 7 - Create a New Forest
docs.text:
Because this is the first Domain Controller in our environment, select:

Add a new forest

Enter the root domain name:

hospital.local

docs.title: What Is a Forest?
docs.text:
A forest is the top-level Active Directory structure that can contain one or more domains.

For this project:

Forest
   │
   └── hospital.local

Our environment only needs one domain, so the architecture remains simple.

In larger organisations, Active Directory architectures can contain multiple domains.

docs.title: Step 8 - Configure Domain Controller Options
docs.text:
The wizard will display Domain Controller options.

For this environment, the server can provide:

  • Domain Name System (DNS)
  • Global Catalog services

You will also be asked to create a:

Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) password

DSRM is used for special Active Directory recovery and maintenance scenarios.

Use a strong lab-specific password and store it safely.

Warning

Do not reuse personal, university or workplace passwords in the lab.

docs.title: Step 9 - Review the DNS Warning
docs.text:
During a new lab-domain installation, the wizard may display DNS-related warnings.

Read the warning rather than automatically assuming the installation has failed.

The new Domain Controller will install and configure DNS services required for the Active Directory environment.

Continue after reviewing the configuration.

docs.title: Step 10 - Review the NetBIOS Domain Name
docs.text:
Windows will generate a NetBIOS domain name.

For example:

HOSPITAL

This allows usernames to be represented in a format such as:

HOSPITAL\emma

The DNS-style domain name remains:

hospital.local

These are two ways of referring to the domain in different contexts.

docs.title: Step 11 - Complete the Prerequisite Check
docs.text:
Before installation continues, Windows performs prerequisite checks.

The wizard checks whether the server is ready to become a Domain Controller.

Review any warnings or errors.

If the prerequisite check passes, continue with the installation.

docs.title: Step 12 - Restart the Server
docs.text:
During promotion, Windows configures:

  • Active Directory Domain Services
  • the new domain
  • the directory database
  • DNS integration
  • Domain Controller services

The server will restart.

After the restart, the machine is no longer simply a standalone Windows Server.

It is now a Domain Controller for the Active Directory domain.

docs.title: Step 13 - Sign In to the Domain
docs.text:
After restart, examine the sign-in screen.

You should now see the domain identity context.

For example:

HOSPITAL\Administrator

This is different from signing into a purely local machine account.

docs.title: Step 14 - Verify Active Directory
docs.text:
Open:

Server Manager → Tools

You should now see administrative tools such as:

  • Active Directory Users and Computers
  • Active Directory Administrative Center
  • DNS
  • Active Directory Domains and Trusts
  • Active Directory Sites and Services

Open:

Active Directory Users and Computers

You should see the domain:

hospital.local

This confirms that the Active Directory structure exists.

docs.title: Step 15 - Verify Active Directory with PowerShell
docs.text:
PowerShell provides another way to inspect the environment.

Open PowerShell as Administrator.

Run:

Get-ADDomain

This returns information about the Active Directory domain.

You can also run:

Get-ADForest

to inspect the forest.

To inspect the Domain Controller:

Get-ADDomainController

docs.title: Why Use Both GUI and PowerShell?
docs.text: Enterprise administrators often use both.

docs.title: GUI tools
docs.text:
Useful for:

  • learning the structure
  • visual inspection
  • occasional administration
  • exploring object properties

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
Useful for:

  • automation
  • repeatable tasks
  • bulk operations
  • troubleshooting
  • scripting

Throughout this project, we will use both approaches.

docs.title: Step 16 - Open DNS Manager
docs.text:
From Server Manager, open:

Tools → DNS

You should see DNS zones associated with the Active Directory environment.

The domain:

hospital.local

should now be represented in DNS.

This is an important moment in the project because Active Directory and DNS are now working together.

docs.title: Step 17 - Test Domain DNS
docs.text:
Open PowerShell or Command Prompt.

Try:

nslookup hospital.local

You can also inspect the configured DNS server:

ipconfig /all

After promotion, the Domain Controller will normally use its own DNS service for Active Directory name resolution.

docs.title: Organizational Units
docs.text:
Active Directory contains many types of objects.

One particularly useful structure is the Organizational Unit, or OU.

OUs allow administrators to organise directory objects logically.

For example:

hospital.local
      │
      ├── Doctors
      ├── Nurses
      ├── Pharmacy
      └── IT

An OU is primarily an administrative container.

It is not the same thing as a Security Group.

docs.title: OU vs Security Group
docs.text: This distinction is extremely important.

docs.title: Organizational Unit
docs.text:
Used primarily to organise and administer objects.

Example:

OU: Nurses
    ├── Emma Wilson
    └── Sarah Jones

docs.title: Security Group
docs.text:
Used to assign permissions or represent access membership.

Example:

Security Group: GG-Nurses
       │
       ├── Emma Wilson
       └── Sarah Jones
              ↓
       Clinical Folder Access

So:

OU
↓
Organisation / Administration

Security Group
↓
Access / Authorization

We will explore Security Groups properly in the next lesson.

docs.title: Step 18 - Create the Hospital OUs
docs.text:
Open:

Active Directory Users and Computers

Right-click the domain:

hospital.local

Choose:

New → Organizational Unit

Create example OUs such as:

Doctors
Nurses
Pharmacy
IT

Your structure may look like:

hospital.local
      │
      ├── Doctors
      ├── Nurses
      ├── Pharmacy
      └── IT

These OUs will later contain the simulated hospital identities.

docs.title: Why Organise Identities?
docs.text:
Imagine managing thousands of identities in one flat list.

That quickly becomes difficult.

A directory structure makes it easier to understand where objects belong and where administrative rules may be applied.

For example:

Hospital
   │
   ├── Clinical Staff
   │      ├── Doctors
   │      └── Nurses
   │
   └── Technical Staff
          └── IT

The exact structure will depend on an organisation's requirements.

docs.title: How Active Directory Stores Identities
docs.text:
An Active Directory user is more than a username.

A directory object can contain information such as:

  • first name
  • surname
  • username
  • email address
  • department
  • group memberships
  • password-related attributes
  • account status

Later, applications can query some of this information using protocols such as LDAP.

That is how this Active Directory lesson connects to the future integration stage.

docs.title: Active Directory and LDAP
docs.text:
LDAP stands for Lightweight Directory Access Protocol.

Active Directory supports LDAP so that systems can communicate with the directory.

Later our Ubuntu integration machine will be able to make requests such as:

Ubuntu Application
       │
       │ LDAP
       │ TCP 389
       ▼
Domain Controller
       │
       ▼
Active Directory
       │
       └── User information

This is where our project moves from infrastructure administration toward software integration.

docs.title: How Authentication Will Eventually Work
docs.text:
A simplified authentication flow may look like:

User
 │
 │ Credentials
 ▼
Application
 │
 │ Authentication request
 ▼
Active Directory
 │
 ├── Valid credentials → Success
 │
 └── Invalid credentials → Failure

Authentication only confirms identity.

The application may still need group membership or other information to make authorization decisions.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Active Directory
docs.text:
When Active Directory does not work, avoid assuming that AD DS itself is broken.

Check the surrounding dependencies.

docs.title: Layer 1 - Server
docs.text:
Is Windows Server running?

hostname

docs.title: Layer 2 - Network
docs.text:
Does the server have the correct IP configuration?

ipconfig /all

docs.title: Layer 3 - DNS
docs.text:
Can the domain be resolved?

nslookup hospital.local

docs.title: Layer 4 - Active Directory
docs.text:
Can PowerShell query the domain?

Get-ADDomain

docs.title: Layer 5 - Service or Application
docs.text:
Can the external system reach the required service?

Later we may test ports such as:

DNS   → TCP/UDP 53
LDAP  → TCP 389
LDAPS → TCP 636
SMB   → TCP 445

This layered troubleshooting approach prevents us from blaming an application when the actual problem exists lower in the infrastructure.

docs.title: Time Synchronisation
docs.text:
Accurate time is important in domain environments.

Authentication systems such as Kerberos are sensitive to significant differences between system clocks.

Check the Windows time service with:

w32tm /query /status

If authentication behaves unexpectedly, time synchronization should be part of the investigation.

docs.title: What You Should Understand
docs.text:
Before continuing, make sure you can explain:

What is Active Directory?

A centralized directory system used to manage identities, computers and other objects in a Windows enterprise environment.

What is AD DS?

The Windows Server role that provides Active Directory Domain Services.

What is a Domain Controller?

A server running AD DS that provides directory and authentication services for a domain.

What is a domain?

A logical Active Directory environment containing centrally managed identities and resources.

What is a forest?

The top-level Active Directory structure that can contain one or more domains.

Why does Active Directory depend on DNS?

Because clients use DNS to locate domain services, including Domain Controllers.

What is an OU?

A container used to organise and administer Active Directory objects.

Is an OU the same as a Security Group?

No.

OUs organise objects.

Security Groups are commonly used to assign permissions and represent authorization membership.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Before moving on, confirm that:

  • AD DS is installed
  • Windows Server has been promoted to a Domain Controller
  • the hospital.local domain exists
  • DNS is installed and working
  • Active Directory Users and Computers opens
  • Get-ADDomain returns domain information
  • Get-ADForest returns forest information
  • the hospital OUs exist
  • you understand the difference between an OU and a Security Group

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
Imagine a new nurse called Emma Wilson joins the hospital.

Before creating anything, decide:

  1. Where should her Active Directory user object be organised?
  2. What determines whether she is allowed to access a clinical folder?
  3. Which concept verifies her identity?
  4. Which concept controls what she can access?

A possible answer is:

Emma Wilson
    │
    ├── User object → Nurses OU
    │
    ├── Authentication → confirms identity
    │
    └── Security Group membership
                    ↓
                Authorization
                    ↓
             Resource access

In the next lesson, you will build exactly this model.

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text:
The hospital now has a centralized identity system.

Next, we will create users and Security Groups, then use group membership to control access.

Continue to Access Management →

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
In this lesson, you will create and manage identities inside Active Directory and use Security Groups to control access.

By the end of the lesson, you should understand:

  • user provisioning
  • Security Groups
  • group membership
  • authentication
  • authorization
  • least privilege
  • role-based access
  • account disabling
  • deprovisioning
  • how to verify access decisions

docs.title: Where We Are
docs.text:
The environment now contains a Domain Controller running Active Directory:

Windows Server
      │
      ├── Active Directory
      ├── DNS
      └── hospital.local

We also created Organizational Units to organise hospital identities.

Now we will begin creating the identities themselves.

A simplified structure might look like:

hospital.local
      │
      ├── Doctors
      ├── Nurses
      ├── Pharmacy
      └── IT

But organising users is only part of Identity and Access Management.

We must also decide:

What should each identity be allowed to access?

docs.title: Identity and Access Management
docs.text: Identity and Access Management, often shortened to IAM, combines two important questions:

docs.title: Identity
docs.text: Who is the user?

docs.title: Access
docs.text:
What should that user be allowed to do?

For example:

Emma Wilson
     │
     ├── Identity: Nurse
     │
     └── Access: Nursing resources

Active Directory helps us manage both identity information and access-related group memberships.

docs.title: Authentication vs Authorization
docs.text: These concepts must remain separate.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Authentication verifies identity.

Emma enters credentials
        ↓
Active Directory
        ↓
Credentials valid
        ↓
Authenticated

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
Authorization determines what the authenticated identity may access.

Emma
  │
  ├── Authenticated
  │
  └── Member of GG-Nurses
              ↓
       Nursing resource
              ↓
          Access granted

A user may successfully authenticate and still receive:

Access Denied

That is not necessarily an authentication failure.

It may be an authorization decision.

docs.title: What Is Provisioning?
docs.text:
Provisioning is the process of creating and configuring an identity so that a person or system receives the access required for their role.

A simplified onboarding process could be:

Employee joins hospital
        ↓
Create identity
        ↓
Place in correct OU
        ↓
Assign Security Groups
        ↓
Provide required access
        ↓
User starts work

Provisioning should be controlled and repeatable.

docs.title: Example Hospital Identities
docs.text:
For this project, we can create fictional users such as:

User Role Emma Wilson Nurse Mike Smith Doctor David King Pharmacy Solomon Prince IT Marie DelGloria No clinical access assigned

These accounts are fictional and exist only for the simulated environment.

docs.title: Step 1 - Open Active Directory Users and Computers
docs.text:
On the Domain Controller, open:

Server Manager → Tools → Active Directory Users and Computers

Expand:

hospital.local

You should see the Organizational Units created previously.

docs.title: Step 2 - Create a User
docs.text:
Open the appropriate OU.

For example:

Nurses

Right-click the OU and select:

New → User

Create a fictional identity.

Example:

First name: Emma
Last name: Wilson
User logon name: emma.wilson

The resulting identity might be represented as:

emma.wilson@hospital.local

docs.title: Step 3 - Configure the Initial Password
docs.text:
Active Directory will ask you to create a password.

For a simulated employee account, you may choose:

User must change password at next logon

This allows the administrator to provide a temporary password without keeping that password permanently.

Warning

Never use real personal, university or workplace passwords in this project.

Use credentials created specifically for the simulated environment.

docs.title: Password Policies
docs.text:
Active Directory may enforce password rules.

For example, the environment may require:

  • minimum password length
  • password complexity
  • password history
  • account lockout rules

If Active Directory rejects a password, investigate the policy rather than repeatedly guessing.

Password policy is part of identity security.

docs.title: Step 4 - Create the Remaining Users
docs.text:
Create additional fictional identities.

For example:

Doctors OU
└── Mike Smith

Nurses OU
└── Emma Wilson

Pharmacy OU
└── David King

IT OU
└── Solomon Prince

You may also create another identity that intentionally receives no departmental Security Group.

For example:

Marie DelGloria

We will use this account to demonstrate authorization.

docs.title: Step 5 - Verify Users with PowerShell
docs.text:
Open PowerShell as Administrator.

To list users:

Get-ADUser -Filter *

To search for one user:

Get-ADUser -Identity emma.wilson

PowerShell gives us another way to inspect Active Directory without relying only on the GUI.

docs.title: What Is a Security Group?
docs.text:
A Security Group allows multiple identities to be treated as one access-control unit.

Instead of giving permissions directly to every nurse:

Emma → Clinical Folder
Sarah → Clinical Folder
John → Clinical Folder
Anna → Clinical Folder

we can create:

GG-Nurses
    │
    ├── Emma
    ├── Sarah
    ├── John
    └── Anna
         │
         ▼
   Clinical Folder

We assign the permission to the group.

Users receive access by becoming members of that group.

docs.title: Why Use Groups?
docs.text:
Group-based access is easier to manage and audit.

Imagine 100 nurses need the same resource.

Without groups:

100 users
   ↓
100 individual permission assignments

With a group:

100 users
   ↓
GG-Nurses
   ↓
1 permission assignment

This is much easier to maintain.

docs.title: Step 6 - Create Security Groups
docs.text:
In Active Directory Users and Computers, create Security Groups for the hospital roles.

For example:

GG-Doctors
GG-Nurses
GG-Pharmacy
GG-IT

The GG naming convention can be used to indicate a Global Group.

Naming conventions vary between organisations.

What matters is that names remain:

  • understandable
  • consistent
  • meaningful

docs.title: Step 7 - Add Users to Groups
docs.text:
Add each fictional identity to the group appropriate for their role.

For example:

Emma Wilson
    ↓
GG-Nurses

Mike Smith
    ↓
GG-Doctors

David King
    ↓
GG-Pharmacy

Solomon Prince
    ↓
GG-IT

Leave Marie outside these groups for now.

This gives us an account that can authenticate but does not have the same authorization as the clinical users.

docs.title: Step 8 - Verify Group Membership
docs.text:
Using the GUI:

  1. Open the user
  2. Select Properties
  3. Open Member Of

You should see the Security Groups assigned to the account.

You can also verify using PowerShell:

Get-ADPrincipalGroupMembership emma.wilson

This shows the groups associated with Emma's identity.

docs.title: A Simple Access Model
docs.text:
We can now model access like this:

Emma Wilson
    │
    └── GG-Nurses
             │
             ▼
       Nursing Resource

For Mike:

Mike Smith
    │
    └── GG-Doctors
             │
             ▼
        Doctor Resource

For Marie:

Marie DelGloria
       │
       ├── Valid account
       └── Not in GG-Nurses
                    │
                    ▼
              Nursing Resource
                    │
                    ▼
               Access Denied

This demonstrates the difference between authentication and authorization.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
The Principle of Least Privilege means that identities should receive only the access required to perform their responsibilities.

A nurse may need access to nursing resources.

That does not automatically mean the nurse should receive:

  • Domain Administrator access
  • IT administration access
  • pharmacy administration access
  • access to every server
  • access to every file share

A simplified model is:

User
 ↓
Job requirement
 ↓
Minimum necessary access

Not:

User
 ↓
Give everything

docs.title: Why Least Privilege Matters
docs.text:
Excessive permissions increase risk.

If an account is:

  • compromised
  • misused
  • incorrectly configured

the damage is limited when the account only has the permissions required for its role.

Least privilege is therefore both an operational and security principle.

docs.title: Role-Based Access
docs.text:
Many organisations assign access according to roles.

For example:

Role: Nurse
    ↓
GG-Nurses
    ↓
Nursing permissions

If Emma later changes role:

Nurse
  ↓
Doctor

the administrator should review and change her access rather than simply adding more permissions indefinitely.

docs.title: Avoid Permission Accumulation
docs.text:
Consider this example:

Emma starts as Nurse
       ↓
Gets Nurses access

Emma moves to Pharmacy
       ↓
Gets Pharmacy access
```

If nobody removes the old group:

~~~text
Emma
 ├── Nurses access
 └── Pharmacy access

She may now have more access than her current role requires.

This is sometimes described as privilege accumulation or access creep.

Access should therefore be reviewed when roles change.

docs.title: Step 9 - Modify a User's Access
docs.text:
Suppose a fictional employee transfers from one department to another.

Review:

  1. the user's current groups
  2. the groups required for the new role
  3. groups that are no longer required

Remove unnecessary memberships.

Add only the groups required for the new responsibilities.

Then verify the result.

docs.title: Joiner, Mover, Leaver
docs.text: Identity lifecycle management is often described using three stages.

docs.title: Joiner
docs.text:
A new employee arrives.

Joiner
  ↓
Create account
  ↓
Assign required access

docs.title: Mover
docs.text:
An employee changes role.

Mover
  ↓
Review existing access
  ↓
Remove unnecessary permissions
  ↓
Add new required access

docs.title: Leaver
docs.text:
An employee leaves the organisation.

Leaver
  ↓
Disable access
  ↓
Remove sensitive memberships
  ↓
Complete deprovisioning

This lifecycle is extremely important in enterprise IAM.

docs.title: What Is Deprovisioning?
docs.text:
Deprovisioning removes or disables access when an identity should no longer be active.

For example, if a staff member leaves the hospital:

Employee leaves
      ↓
Disable account
      ↓
Remove access
      ↓
Review ownership/resources
      ↓
Account handled according to policy

Simply forgetting the account creates a security risk.

docs.title: Step 10 - Disable a User Account
docs.text:
In Active Directory Users and Computers:

  1. locate the user
  2. right-click the account
  3. select Disable Account

A disabled account remains in Active Directory but cannot normally authenticate.

This can be safer than immediately deleting an account because administrators may need to preserve information during an offboarding process.

docs.title: Disable vs Delete
docs.text: These actions are different.

docs.title: Disable
docs.text:
Account exists
      ↓
Authentication blocked

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
Directory object removed

In real organisations, offboarding procedures determine when accounts are disabled, retained, archived or deleted.

Do not assume deletion should always be immediate.

docs.title: Disable an Account with PowerShell
docs.text:
You can disable an account using:

Disable-ADAccount -Identity marie.delgloria

You can verify whether an account is enabled with:

Get-ADUser -Identity marie.delgloria -Properties Enabled

docs.title: Enable an Account
docs.text:
If an account was disabled for testing and needs to be restored:

Enable-ADAccount -Identity marie.delgloria

Always verify that restoring an account is actually appropriate before enabling it.

docs.title: Inspect Group Membership with PowerShell
docs.text:
You can inspect a user:

Get-ADUser -Identity emma.wilson

You can inspect the groups they belong to:

Get-ADPrincipalGroupMembership emma.wilson

You can inspect members of a group:

Get-ADGroupMember -Identity GG-Nurses

These commands are useful during troubleshooting.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Access
docs.text:
Suppose Emma reports:

I can sign in, but I cannot access the nursing resource.

Do not immediately reset her password.

Work through the problem logically.

docs.title: Step 1 - Can she authenticate?
docs.text:
Can Emma sign in successfully?

If yes, her credentials may not be the problem.

docs.title: Step 2 - Is the account enabled?
docs.text: Get-ADUser emma.wilson -Properties Enabled

docs.title: Step 3 - Is she in the required group?
docs.text:
Get-ADPrincipalGroupMembership emma.wilson

Look for:

GG-Nurses

docs.title: Step 4 - Does the group have permission?
docs.text: Even if Emma is in the correct group, the group itself must be authorized to the resource.

docs.title: Step 5 - Has the access change taken effect?
docs.text: Some access changes may require a new logon session or refreshed authentication token before they are reflected everywhere.

docs.title: A Better Troubleshooting Question
docs.text:
Instead of asking:

Why can't the user access the folder?

Break the problem into layers:

Does the identity exist?
        ↓
Is the account enabled?
        ↓
Can the user authenticate?
        ↓
Is the user in the correct group?
        ↓
Does that group have permission?
        ↓
Can the resource be reached?

This makes troubleshooting much more systematic.

docs.title: Why Not Give Permissions Directly to Users?
docs.text:
Direct user permissions may work technically.

But they become difficult to manage at scale.

For example:

Emma → permission
Mike → permission
David → permission
Solomon → permission
```

becomes harder to understand later.

A group model is clearer:

~~~text
Users
  ↓
Security Groups
  ↓
Permissions
  ↓
Resources

This creates separation between:

Who the users are

and:

What access their roles receive

docs.title: Identity vs Group vs Permission
docs.text:
Keep these three layers separate.

Identity
Emma Wilson
     ↓
Group
GG-Nurses
     ↓
Permission
Read / Modify
     ↓
Resource
Clinical Folder

This model will become very important in the next lesson when we configure SMB and NTFS permissions.

docs.title: Service Accounts
docs.text:
Not every Active Directory identity represents a human.

Applications and services may also require identities.

These are commonly called service accounts.

A service account may later allow our Ubuntu application to communicate with Active Directory.

For example:

Ubuntu Application
        │
        │ Uses service identity
        ▼
Active Directory
        │
        └── Directory query

Service accounts should also follow least privilege.

An application that only needs to read directory information should not automatically receive Domain Administrator privileges.

docs.title: What You Should Understand
docs.text:
Before continuing, make sure you can explain:

What is provisioning?

Creating and configuring an identity with the access required for its role.

What is authorization?

Determining what an authenticated identity is allowed to access.

Why use Security Groups?

They allow permissions to be managed through reusable access groups instead of assigning access individually to every user.

What is least privilege?

Giving an identity only the permissions needed to perform its responsibilities.

What is deprovisioning?

Removing or disabling access when it is no longer required.

What is the Joiner-Mover-Leaver lifecycle?

A model for managing access when users join an organisation, change roles or leave.

Why might an account be disabled instead of immediately deleted?

Because organisations may need to block access while temporarily preserving the directory object for operational, security or policy reasons.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Before continuing, confirm that:

  • fictional Active Directory users exist
  • users are organised appropriately
  • Security Groups exist
  • users have been added to the correct groups
  • group membership can be checked
  • you understand authentication vs authorization
  • you understand least privilege
  • you can disable an account
  • you understand provisioning and deprovisioning
  • you understand Joiner, Mover and Leaver processes

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
Consider these two users:

Emma Wilson
Account: Enabled
Password: Valid
Group: GG-Nurses

Marie DelGloria
Account: Enabled
Password: Valid
Group: None

Both attempt to access a resource configured for GG-Nurses.

Emma receives:

Access Granted

Marie receives:

Access Denied

Answer these questions:

  1. Did both users authenticate successfully?
  2. Why did Marie receive Access Denied?
  3. Is this an authentication problem or an authorization problem?
  4. What would you check before adding Marie to GG-Nurses?

The important answer to question 4 is:

Confirm that Marie's actual job role requires that access.

Never fix an access problem by granting permissions before verifying that the user should have them.

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text:
We now have identities and Security Groups.

Next, we will connect those groups to a real resource by creating an SMB file share and applying group-based permissions.

Continue to SMB & Permissions →

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
In this lesson, you will create a shared folder on Windows Server and use Active Directory Security Groups to control who can access it.

By the end of the lesson, you should understand:

  • what SMB is
  • what a network share is
  • the difference between Share and NTFS permissions
  • how Active Directory groups can control resource access
  • how authentication and authorization appear in a real access test
  • why permissions should normally be assigned to groups rather than individual users
  • how to troubleshoot an Access Denied error

docs.title: Where We Are
docs.text:
Our environment now contains:

Active Directory
      │
      ├── Users
      │
      └── Security Groups
              │
              ├── GG-Nurses
              ├── GG-Doctors
              ├── GG-Pharmacy
              └── GG-IT

The groups exist, but they do not yet control a real resource.

In this lesson, we will connect a Security Group to a shared folder.

For example:

Emma Wilson
     │
     └── GG-Nurses
              │
              ▼
       Clinical Share
              │
              ▼
         Access Granted

while another authenticated user may receive:

Marie DelGloria
       │
       └── Not a member of GG-Nurses
                    │
                    ▼
              Clinical Share
                    │
                    ▼
               Access Denied

This turns our IAM model into a real authorization test.

docs.title: What Is SMB?
docs.text:
SMB stands for Server Message Block.

It is a network protocol commonly used by Windows systems to provide access to resources such as:

  • shared folders
  • files
  • printers

A simplified SMB connection looks like:

Client Computer
      │
      │ SMB
      │ TCP 445
      ▼
Windows Server
      │
      └── Shared Folder

The modern SMB service normally uses:

TCP 445

docs.title: What Is a Network Share?
docs.text:
A folder normally exists on one computer.

For example:

C:\HospitalData\Clinical

A network share makes that folder available to authorized systems over the network.

It might be accessed using a UNC path such as:

\\DC01\Clinical

or:

\\<server-ip>\Clinical

docs.title: What Is a UNC Path?
docs.text:
UNC stands for Universal Naming Convention.

A UNC path identifies a network resource.

The general format is:

\\ServerName\ShareName

For example:

\\DC01\Clinical

The first component identifies the server.

The second identifies the shared resource.

docs.title: Our Access Model
docs.text:
For this lesson, imagine that the hospital has a shared clinical folder intended for nursing staff.

We want:

GG-Nurses
    │
    ▼
Clinical Share
    │
    └── Access

The important point is that we do not assign the permission directly to Emma.

Instead:

Emma
  ↓
GG-Nurses
  ↓
Permission
  ↓
Clinical Share

This makes access easier to manage.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
Confirm that:

  • Active Directory is running
  • the Security Groups exist
  • at least one test user belongs to GG-Nurses
  • another test user exists outside GG-Nurses
  • Windows Server networking is working

You can verify the Nurses group with:

Get-ADGroup -Identity GG-Nurses

To inspect its members:

Get-ADGroupMember -Identity GG-Nurses

docs.title: Step 1 - Create the Folder
docs.text:
On Windows Server, create a folder for the simulated resource.

For example:

C:\HospitalData\Clinical

You can create it through File Explorer.

Or with PowerShell:

New-Item -Path "C:\HospitalData\Clinical" -ItemType Directory

docs.title: Step 2 - Add a Test File
docs.text:
Inside the folder, create a harmless test file.

For example:

welcome.txt

The file might contain:

This is a simulated clinical resource.
No real patient information is stored here.

Warning

Never place real patient data, workplace information, passwords or production credentials inside this learning environment.

docs.title: Step 3 - Share the Folder
docs.text:
Right-click the Clinical folder.

Open:

Properties → Sharing

Then choose:

Advanced Sharing

Enable:

Share this folder

Use a simple share name such as:

Clinical

The network path will eventually resemble:

\\DC01\Clinical

Your server name may be different.

docs.title: Step 4 - Understand Share Permissions
docs.text:
A Windows file share can have Share Permissions.

Examples include:

  • Read
  • Change
  • Full Control

Share permissions apply when the resource is accessed through SMB over the network.

For example:

Client
   │
   │ SMB
   ▼
Share Permissions
   │
   ▼
Shared Folder

docs.title: Step 5 - Understand NTFS Permissions
docs.text:
The folder also exists on an NTFS filesystem.

NTFS permissions can control actions such as:

  • Read
  • Write
  • Modify
  • Full Control

These permissions apply to the files and folders themselves.

So Windows may evaluate two permission layers when a user accesses the folder through the network:

User
 ↓
SMB Share Permission
 ↓
NTFS Permission
 ↓
Resource

docs.title: Share vs NTFS Permissions
docs.text: This distinction is important.

docs.title: Share Permissions
docs.text: Apply to access through the network share.

docs.title: NTFS Permissions
docs.text:
Apply to the actual filesystem object.

When both apply, the user does not gain more access simply because one layer is permissive.

The effective access must satisfy the restrictions imposed by the relevant permission layers.

For example:

Share:
Read + Change

NTFS:
Read only

Result:
User cannot modify the file

This is why both layers should be checked during troubleshooting.

docs.title: Step 6 - Assign Access to the Security Group
docs.text:
Instead of assigning access directly to Emma Wilson, assign it to:

GG-Nurses

For a learning environment, you might allow the group to:

Read
or
Modify

depending on the scenario you want to test.

The design should remain:

Resource
   ↑
Permission
   ↑
GG-Nurses
   ↑
Users

docs.title: Why Not Assign the Permission Directly to Emma?
docs.text:
This would technically work:

Clinical
   ↑
Emma Wilson

But imagine 200 nurses.

You would eventually have:

Clinical
   ├── Emma
   ├── Sarah
   ├── James
   ├── Anna
   ├── John
   └── ...

That becomes difficult to maintain.

A group model is cleaner:

Clinical
   ↑
GG-Nurses
   ↑
200 nurses

When someone joins the nursing team, you update their group membership.

You do not need to redesign the resource permissions.

docs.title: Step 7 - Review NTFS Security
docs.text:
Open:

Clinical → Properties → Security

Review the identities currently listed.

Depending on your environment, inherited entries may already exist.

Do not remove system or administrative permissions without understanding why they exist.

Add:

GG-Nurses

and assign the level of access required for the exercise.

For example:

Read & execute
List folder contents
Read

or, if the exercise requires users to modify files:

Modify

docs.title: Least Privilege Still Applies
docs.text:
Do not automatically grant:

Full Control

just because it is convenient.

Ask:

What does this group actually need to do?

If nurses only need to read the resource:

GG-Nurses
     ↓
Read

may be more appropriate than:

GG-Nurses
     ↓
Full Control

This is the Principle of Least Privilege applied to files.

docs.title: Step 8 - Verify the Share
docs.text:
Open PowerShell.

Run:

Get-SmbShare

You should see the new share.

For more information:

Get-SmbShare -Name Clinical

You can inspect share permissions with:

Get-SmbShareAccess -Name Clinical

docs.title: Step 9 - Check That SMB Is Listening
docs.text:
SMB normally uses TCP port 445.

From another Windows system, you can test whether the server accepts connections to that port with:

Test-NetConnection <server-ip> -Port 445

A successful result may include:

TcpTestSucceeded : True

This tells you that the SMB service can be reached at the network layer.

It does not prove that the user is authorized to the folder.

docs.title: Connectivity vs Authorization
docs.text: These are separate questions.

docs.title: Connectivity
docs.text:
Can the client reach the SMB service?

Client
  ↓
TCP 445
  ↓
Server

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Can the server verify the user's identity?

Credentials
    ↓
Active Directory
    ↓
Authenticated

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
Is that authenticated user allowed to access this share?

Authenticated User
       ↓
Group Membership
       ↓
Permissions
       ↓
Granted / Denied

This separation is essential during troubleshooting.

docs.title: Step 10 - Test an Authorized User
docs.text:
Use a test user who belongs to:

GG-Nurses

For example:

Emma Wilson

From a Windows client or appropriate test session, access:

\\DC01\Clinical

or use the actual server name in your environment.

If Emma:

  1. authenticates successfully
  2. belongs to GG-Nurses
  3. and GG-Nurses has the required permissions

the expected result is:

Access Granted

docs.title: Step 11 - Test an Unauthorized User
docs.text:
Now use an account that is not a member of GG-Nurses.

For example:

Marie DelGloria

Assume:

Account exists
Password is valid
Account is enabled

Marie may successfully authenticate.

But when she attempts:

\\DC01\Clinical

the expected result is:

Access Denied

if no other permission grants her access.

docs.title: Why This Test Matters
docs.text:
Compare the two users:

Emma
 ├── Account valid
 ├── Authentication successful
 └── GG-Nurses member
           ↓
      Access Granted


Marie
 ├── Account valid
 ├── Authentication successful
 └── Not in GG-Nurses
           ↓
       Access Denied

The difference is not identity verification.

The difference is authorization.

docs.title: Authentication Success Does Not Mean Access Success
docs.text:
This is a common troubleshooting mistake.

Imagine a user says:

My password works, but I cannot open the folder.

Resetting the password may not solve anything.

The identity may already be authenticated.

The actual problem may be:

  • missing group membership
  • incorrect NTFS permissions
  • incorrect share permissions
  • access token not refreshed
  • wrong resource path

docs.title: Step 12 - Verify Group Membership
docs.text:
Check whether the user belongs to the required group:

Get-ADPrincipalGroupMembership emma.wilson

Or inspect the group:

Get-ADGroupMember GG-Nurses

You should be able to determine whether the authorization relationship exists:

Emma
  ↓
GG-Nurses

docs.title: Step 13 - Test a Permission Change
docs.text:
For a controlled learning exercise, remove a test user from GG-Nurses.

For example:

Remove-ADGroupMember -Identity GG-Nurses -Members emma.wilson

PowerShell will normally ask you to confirm the change.

After the user's authentication context has been refreshed appropriately, test access again.

The expected relationship becomes:

Emma
  │
  └── No GG-Nurses membership
             ↓
        Clinical Share
             ↓
         Access Denied

You can then restore the membership:

Add-ADGroupMember -Identity GG-Nurses -Members emma.wilson

This demonstrates that access comes from group membership rather than from Emma's identity being manually attached to the folder.

docs.title: Why Access Changes May Not Appear Immediately
docs.text:
When users authenticate, Windows creates an access token containing information such as Security Group memberships.

If a group membership changes while the user is already signed in, the current session may still contain the previous information.

A new sign-in session may therefore be required before some permission changes are reflected.

This is another reason troubleshooting should include the user's current authentication session.

docs.title: Step 14 - Inspect Current SMB Connections
docs.text:
On the server, you can inspect SMB sessions using:

Get-SmbSession

You can also inspect files currently opened through SMB:

Get-SmbOpenFile

These commands can help determine whether clients are actually connected to the server.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Scenario 1
docs.text:
The user reports:

I cannot open \\DC01\Clinical.

Start with the path.

Check:

Is the server name correct?
        ↓
Is the share name correct?
        ↓
Does the share exist?

Verify:

Get-SmbShare -Name Clinical

docs.title: Troubleshooting Scenario 2
docs.text:
The server name cannot be resolved.

Test DNS:

nslookup DC01

If name resolution fails, try to determine whether the issue is DNS rather than SMB.

You can also temporarily compare behavior using the server IP:

\\<server-ip>\Clinical
